question: How do we predict a qualitative response from predictors, and how do logistic regression, LDA, QDA, naive Bayes, KNN and generalized linear models compare?
contributions: Logistic regression incl. multinomial and softmax coding

Analytical and six-scenario simulation comparison of methods
Poisson regression and generalized linear models; Python lab with statsmodels and scikit-learn

limits: Default is simulated with an exaggerated balance-default relationship; the authors say so.
Default confusion matrices are on the 10,000 training observations, not a held-out set; training error is optimistic.
Scenario comparison error rates are only shown as boxplots; text gives rankings, not numbers.
Smarket results are a single 2005 split of 252 days; authors warn to evaluate on a larger test set before trusting QDA's 59.9%.
Poisson model on Bikeshare shows overdispersion, inflating z-values; not corrected (footnote 5).
LDA applied with a dummy-variable predictor (student) violates normality; authors note robustness.
Caravan KNN precision per K is based on tiny counts (3 to 62 predicted).
practices: Do not use linear regression for a qualitative response with more than two classes or when probability estimates matter (Sec 4.2, p.138).
Prefer LDA over logistic regression when classes are well separated or n is small with roughly normal predictors; logistic when normality fails (Sec 4.4, 4.5.1).
Do not judge a classifier by overall error alone when classes are imbalanced; compare to the null classifier and examine the confusion matrix (p.151-152, 186).
Choose the probability threshold from domain costs, not 0.5 by default (p.153-154); in the lab a 0.25 threshold gave 29 predicted buyers vs none at 0.5.
Summarise across thresholds with the ROC curve and AUC (p.154-155).

Use LDA when data are few, QDA when the training set is large or covariances clearly differ, naive Bayes when n is small relative to p, KNN when the boundary is highly non-linear and n >> p (Sec 4.4.3-4.5.2).
Standardise features before KNN since distance depends on scale (p.185).
Treat K in KNN as a tuning parameter chosen by cross-validation (Sec 4.7.6).
Beware confounding: a single-predictor logistic regression can reverse the sign seen in the multiple regression (student, Tables 4.2 vs 4.3).
Use Poisson regression rather than OLS for count responses (non-negative, mean equals variance), checking for overdispersion (Sec 4.6).
